root_cause.text: The firmware tracer passed untrusted format strings directly from the device firmware as the format argument to snprintf without any validation, allowing unsafe format specifiers (e.g., %s, %n, %p) to cause arbitrary memory access, crashes, or other undefined behavior.
root_cause.evidence: CVE description states "Without proper validation, bad firmware could provide format strings with invalid format specifiers (e.g., %s, %p, %n) that could lead to crashes, or other undefined behavior." The patch adds `mlx5_tracer_validate_params()` to reject non-integer/hex specifiers and modifies `mlx5_tracer_print_trace()` to use `"BAD_FORMAT: %s"` for invalid strings instead of using the raw string as a format.

candidates.rationale: Directly passes the untrusted firmware format string as the format argument to snprintf, enabling arbitrary memory access/crash via %s, %n, or %p specifiers.
Passes the untrusted format string to a function that parses it to count parameters; the parsing itself may be unsafe or rely on the untrusted content.
Uses strstr on the untrusted format string to locate replacement patterns; this is part of insufficient sanitization that still leaves other dangerous specifiers unguarded.
The loop condition that processes the untrusted format string for replacements; the loop body continues to operate on the untrusted string without complete validation.
Defines a replacement format string used in an attempt to sanitize %llx, but this does not protect against other unsafe specifiers like %s or %n, leaving the vulnerability.
Declares a stack buffer that will be written to via snprintf with the untrusted format string; if the format string causes corruption (e.g., %n), this buffer is where the damage occurs.
